json.summary: A cheerful street reporter stops a passer-by and asks what he would do first if he won the lottery. The man is a bored, sleepy-eyed smoker in a hoodie. He answers with a rant about wanting a huge box of 10-packs of forks, which he would scatter everywhere. The reporter keeps suggesting glamorous options (sports car, yacht, villa), and each one is cut off by a 'PINÁK?' (a vulgar word for vagina). The man grabs the reporter and screams in a rage about a bolt that should be a hex-head bolt, then flattens him. In the last panel he calmly stands over the reporter's body. The joke is the lottery question set against an absurdly petty, furious obsession with screws, plus a pun on 'five' (ötös = lottery numbers).

characters.name: reporter
characters.description: Thin, grinning street interviewer with a big nose and a microphone. He is relentlessly cheerful and polite at first ('Jónapot uram'), and he uses standard, TV-presenter Hungarian. He ends up grabbed and flattened by the passer-by.

characters.name: passer-by
characters.description: Heavy, bald man in a hoodie with a cigarette and half-closed, bored eyes. He starts out laconic and then escalates into a screaming rant. He speaks in crude colloquial Hungarian, swearing with 'bazmeg' and 'kurva', and keeps saying 'vagod?' ('get it?') as a tic.

panels.description: The reporter holds a microphone, grinning at the viewer. His big speech bubble announces they will wait for the first random passer-by and ask him the question. The tail points to him (r1 is an empty region around his head).
The reporter, on the left, greets the passer-by and asks the lottery question. The bubble tail runs down to his mouth. The passer-by walks past on the right, smoking, hands in his hoodie pocket.

The reporter holds the mic out and rattles off options (sports car, yacht, travel, villa), with small word bubbles floating around him. Each option is followed by 'PINÁK?'. The passer-by raises one hand in an OK-like gesture and answers 'A lottó ötöst? Hm... lássuk csak... hehe... igen!' with the tail leading to him.

The reporter now has his arm around the passer-by, who has put an arm around him and points off to the side with the cigarette-holding hand. The big bubble belongs to the passer-by, who describes the box of forks. The reporter smiles and holds the mic.
The passer-by has his arm around the reporter and points outward with a wild grin. His bubble continues the rant about scattering the forks everywhere. The reporter looks uneasy and squeezed.

The passer-by has turned into a huge, raging monster with a gaping, fanged mouth, screaming about the six-sided bolt. The reporter is being blown back by the shout, and a bolt lies on the ground at the bottom left.
The passer-by is back to normal and stands calmly over the reporter, who lies flattened on the ground. The mic lies on the floor. His bubble finishes the rant with the 'five' pun.

notes: Check the text against the drawings. The transcript's wording (forks, scattering them like a dandelion, a hex bolt) does not match what the panels show, and it reads as if the lines are jumbled. A translator must follow the transcript literally. The tail logic is that the passer-by delivers r13, r15, r16 and r17 as one escalating rant.

Lottó ötös is the Hungarian 5-number lottery ('Ötöslottó', pick 5 of 90). The reporter asks what he would do after winning it. The final line, 'NEM EGY, ÖT!' ('not one, five!'), plays on 'ötös' (five-number lottery) and ties it to the bolts. In English a 'five/fiver' pun may be needed. The underlined 'ÖT' is the stress.

PINÁK? is a vulgar slang word for the female genitals. The reporter says it after every glamorous option (sports car, yacht, travel, villa) as a gag, which implies it is the real thing everyone wants. Keep it crude but comic. It occurs in r4, r8 and r11, and the other options are r3, r6, r7 and r10.
'Randomtibor' (r0) is a joke name for a random passer-by, like 'Joe Random'. 'Tibor' is a common Hungarian male name. The reporter's 'HÁHHÁ! JÓESTÉT!' is an over-the-top, gleeful, TV-host greeting.

The passer-by's speech: 'kurvanagy' = 'whoring big', a vulgar intensifier. 'Vágod?' = 'you get it?' (slang, repeated in r13 and r15). 'Bazmeg' = a mild-to-strong 'fuck / damn' (a contraction of 'baszd meg'), used in r16 and r17. His 'tizes villáskulccsal' (r13) means 10-mm fork wrenches (open-end spanners), which is why the 'villa' ('fork' and 'villa') idea fits. 'Villa' also means villa in the reporter's list (r10), so the wordplay is villa/fork-wrench. Keep the double meaning if possible.

The whole rant is the humour: a lottery winner whose dream is not luxury but a huge box of ten-millimetre spanners, packed to the brim, with thousands of them. He then wants six-sided hex bolts everywhere he reaches ('wherever I reach, there should be one'). It is a handyman's obsession played with rage, and the contrast between the bland interview and the explosion is the punchline.
'Hogyamikor' (r16) is a clumsy, slangy mash of 'hogy amikor' ('so that when'), which marks the speaker as an uneducated, rambling, casual talker. Keep a clumsy, colloquial feel.
No background signs are in the strip. The only visual running gag is the passer-by's escalating body language: bored, then arm-around-shoulder, then monster, then calm again.
